title: "No blame on you today"
hookLine: a grieving father who never despairs, a brother who forgives, and a shirt that brings back sight
carry: forgive one old thing, out loud
tomorrow: the vow and the fruit out of season

cards: The brothers go home without the youngest, and the eldest stays in Egypt, unwilling to face his father. First Yusuf, now his little brother too. Ya'qub turns away, and the Qur'an says his eyes went white with grief.

His sons think he'll grieve himself to death. He answers: “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.” Then he sends them back: look for Yusuf and his brother, and “despair not of the Spirit of Allah.”
They return a third time, poor, begging for grain as charity. The powerful man across the table asks quietly: do you know what you did to Yusuf? They stare.

teach.h: I AM YUSUF, AND THIS IS MY BROTHER.
teach.b: I am Yusuf, he says, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. They threw him in a well, sold him for a few coins, lied to their father with false blood.
After years as a servant and a prisoner, he holds the grain of Egypt, and they stand before him with empty sacks. They admit it: Allah has preferred you over us, and we were wrong.
Yusuf's answer is la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm.
No blame on you today. No reproach, no list of what you did. Then: may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of those who show mercy.
He doesn't make them earn it. He doesn't wait for them to grovel. Then the shirt returns, one last time.
The first came home with false blood. The second, torn from behind, proved him innocent. Now Yusuf sends a third: lay this on my father's face.
Before the caravan arrives, Ya'qub says, I can smell Yusuf.

teach.h: THE THIRD SHIRT: HIS FATHER SEES.
teach.b: The shirt touches his face, and he sees again.
The whole family comes to Egypt. Yusuf raises his parents up beside him, and they all bow down.

teach.h: DESPAIR NOT OF THE SPIRIT OF ALLAH.
teach.b: Yusuf says: “This is the interpretation of my dream of old.” Eleven stars, sun and moon, from day one of this story. And when Yusuf tells the story back, he says Shaytan made trouble between me and my brothers.
Even then, he won't name them as villains. Years later, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have answered his old enemies in Mecca with these same words.

how: Muslims often recall Yusuf's words to his brothers when making peace after a quarrel, and many read Surah Yusuf in full as a story of patience, trust and forgiveness.

o: a debt owed until it has been repaid in full
reproach: rebuking someone with their faults
a formal pardon granted by a king's court

games.q: what's inside the ending — tap the pairs.
p: the dream of old, come true

s: Yusuf makes his brothers beg before he forgives them
his answer is la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm: no blame on you today, and may Allah forgive you.
in the story, Ya'qub's sight comes back when Yusuf's shirt touches his face
Yusuf sends the shirt with his brothers; laid on his father's face, it restores his sight (12:93–96).
when he tells the story back, Yusuf blames his brothers for everything
he says Shaytan made trouble between him and his brothers (12:100).

games.q: Yusuf holds all the power now. the brothers who threw him in a well stand before him, poor and ashamed. what does he say?
o: list everything they did, one by one.
send them away without the grain.
games.why: la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm: no blame on you today. may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful (12:92).

practice: Let one old hurt come up, not the biggest, one that still stings, a sibling's wrong word years ago, and picture their face. Forgive it out loud, to the room; you don't have to feel it all the way, and today is enough.
If you pray, ask Allah to forgive them, the way Yusuf did.

wordCard.voice: Tathrib, reproach: the word Yusuf set aside when he told his brothers, no blame on you today.

orig.note: Arabic, Qur'an 12:92: no reproach on you today.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive one old thing, out loud. Fourteen days of Yusuf, from a dream to a dream come true; tomorrow, Maryam. Day sixty-eight, done.
